metadata.title: Claude, Investigation Memo.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain investigative judgment when it picks up the investigation-memo skill? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a template Claude reads before it starts, not new decision-making power.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (investigation-memo's single SKILL.md: planted, then returned to)

beats.narration_text: The name says 'investigation-memo,' so it sounds like the skill hands Claude judgment. It doesn't — it hands Claude a template. Let's crack open the folder and see what's actually inside.

beats.narration_text: Here's what the name gets you to imagine: Claude with investigative authority — deciding what actually happened, naming who's responsible for it. That's the natural read.

Run the test: delete the folder. The model doesn't get worse at investigations, because it never got better at them. What stops is one template. The judgment was never in Claude — it lived in that file.

Here's the actual machinery. A skill is a folder. Investigation-memo is a folder holding one file, SKILL.md — plain English, no hidden logic. It's the steps for writing up an investigation in a fixed structure. Claude reads it before it starts. That's the whole trick.
The execution model: Claude reads the file top to bottom, then works the steps in the order they appear. No branching, no reordering — unless a step in the file itself says branch.

So the design choice: a skill is a specification, not new judgment. What that buys is uniformity — the same memo structure, every investigation, every time. What it costs is coverage — anything outside those written steps, Claude has no special opinion about.

So investigation-memo never handed Claude judgment about what happened. What it guarantees is this: every time the skill runs, Claude reads the same file and follows the same structure. That mechanical repeat — that's the whole product.

beats.narration_text: That cuts both ways. A thorough memo doesn't prove Claude understood the investigation — it may have just filled in the template's headings. A thin memo doesn't prove nothing's there — it may be a case the steps don't reach. The output is the shape of the template, not the truth of the case.

So — a skill named investigation-memo doesn't hand Claude judgment about what happened. It's a template Claude reads before it starts. Same structure comes out every run, and anything outside those steps is still yours to judge.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into any frontier LLM — Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one document you always structure the same way — an incident report, a status update, a closing summary. Write me a SKILL.md for it in plain English, ordered steps. Then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll write, before you write it. Go deeper: run that SKILL.md on a real case, delete one step, and re-run it — the delta between the two outputs shows you what the template was actually contributing, and where the judgment still has to come from you.
